**One mind, two channels.** Given that the program and the word channel agree, the chance they are jointly wrong is a Bayes factor in four quantities: the misreading weight ρ, the probability γ that the word channel is centered on the compiled reading, the noise odds λ, and the number d of tests on which the wrong labeling actually differs. That conditional probability is at least the floor ργ / (ργ + 1 − ρ). No larger suite undercuts it, and it equals ρ when the words are noise around the same reading. The gap above the floor shrinks as λ^{−d}, and only when the per-test noise is below (q − 1)/q. It shrinks exponentially in the suite size only if γ = 0 and d itself grows linearly with the suite. Chow suites do not have that shape. In the census of binary Moore machines with at most 3 states, complete suites of 11 words still have a wrong machine at depth 1, and padding keeps that depth at 1 on a characteristic sample of 35 words.

**Finite teaching sets.** The literal conjecture is false in both directions. Constant decoders have teaching dimension 1 on a context image of 511 histories. A finite token cache plus an absolute position has unbounded teaching dimension. What survives is Goldman and Kearns on the decoder's actual input: for the class of all decoders of an input-only cache policy, a finite teaching set is equivalent to a finite context image, with one label per pair. Under the pin, the minimum teaching set for input-output exactness is the reachable rows, not every syntactic row (19008 of 46656 three-state tables leave a row unreached) and not a Chow suite (4 rows against 5 words on the hand machine; on all 1054 census machines the slack-0 suite is strictly larger than the row count). That equality is the teaching set of a finite lookup. It is not beyond Goldman and Kearns 1995, Gold 1978, or de la Higuera 1997.
